title: Caching & Prefetching Strategy for Mobile Clients
summary: Multi-layer client caching from memory to disk to CDN, invalidation strategies a mobile client can actually use, and predictive prefetch — the client-side application of general caching theory.

slides.markdown:
General caching theory — eviction policies, TTLs, cache-aside vs write-through — lives in [System Design](caching-fundamentals). This topic is the client-side application: a mobile app sits at the end of a request's path through **several** independent cache layers before it ever reaches an origin server, and the client itself is one more layer on top of all of them, with its own memory/disk trade-offs and its own invalidation problem to solve.

Getting this right is what makes a feed scroll instantly on a re-visit and an image never re-download twice; getting it wrong is either a UI perpetually re-fetching data it already has, or — worse — a UI confidently showing data that's actually stale and wrong.

slides.subTitle: memory, disk, CDN, origin
slides.markdown:
A single image request on a well-built app can be satisfied at any of four points, each progressively slower and more expensive to fall back to:

- **In-memory cache** — fastest, but volatile (cleared on app termination, limited by available RAM), typically the recently-viewed subset of images/data.
- **Disk cache** — survives app restarts, much larger capacity than memory, but slower to read than memory (real disk I/O, even on fast mobile storage).
- **CDN** — if memory and disk both miss, the request goes out over the network but ideally terminates at a geographically-close edge server rather than the origin, still far faster than a cross-continent round trip.
- **Origin server** — the slowest, most expensive path, hit only when every faster layer missed.

The app's job is checking each layer in order and populating the faster layers on a slower-layer hit, so the *next* request for the same data climbs the hierarchy.

slides.sectionTitle: Cache invalidation strategies a mobile client can use
slides.markdown:
| | Time-based expiry | Server-driven cache headers | Push-invalidation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | client discards after a fixed TTL regardless of whether data actually changed | server response includes ETag/Last-Modified or Cache-Control, client revalidates accordingly | server proactively notifies the client (push notification, silent push) that specific cached data is now stale |
| Freshness | approximate — can serve stale data within the TTL window, or refetch unchanged data after it | accurate — a conditional request (If-None-Match) confirms freshness cheaply, often with a 304 and no body transfer | most accurate, but needs infrastructure (push delivery) and only makes sense for data whose staleness genuinely matters in real time |
| Simplicity | simplest to implement | moderate, standard HTTP mechanism | most complex, real infrastructure cost |

Most mobile apps combine time-based expiry as a baseline with server-driven headers for anything where an unnecessary refetch is wasteful (a large, rarely-changing image) — push-invalidation is reserved for data where staleness has a real, immediate cost (a live inventory count, a price that just changed).

The right choice is genuinely data-dependent, and picking one strategy for the entire app is a common oversimplification. A product's category listing that changes a few times a day tolerates a generous time-based TTL just fine. A user's own cart total, which they'd notice being wrong immediately, deserves server-driven revalidation on every relevant screen visit rather than trusting a TTL window. A price that a promotion just changed, where showing the old price risks an actual support ticket or a broken checkout, is the rare case that justifies push-invalidation's real infrastructure cost.

The practical exercise for any given piece of cached data: what's the actual cost of showing it stale for N seconds/minutes, and does that cost justify the complexity of a more accurate (and more expensive to implement) invalidation strategy?

slides.subTitle: loading the next likely screen before the user asks
slides.markdown:
**Prefetching** is speculatively loading data or content the user hasn't explicitly requested yet, based on a reasonable prediction of what they're about to need: the next page of a feed as they approach the bottom of the current one, a product's detail data as their finger hovers/taps toward its thumbnail, the next few items in a video queue.

The trade-off is explicit: prefetching spends bandwidth and battery on a prediction that might be wrong (the user navigates elsewhere instead), in exchange for eliminating a visible loading delay when the prediction is right. That trade generally favors prefetching for high-confidence predictions (the very next page of a feed the user is actively scrolling toward) and disfavors it for low-confidence, expensive ones (preemptively downloading full-resolution images for every item in a long list on the chance the user might tap one) — confidence and cost both matter to whether a specific prefetch is worth it.

slides.sectionTitle: An image loader with two cache tiers
slides.markdown:
```kotlin
suspend fun loadImage(url: String): Bitmap {
    memoryCache.get(url)?.let { return it }

    diskCache.get(url)?.let { bitmap ->
        memoryCache.put(url, bitmap)   // promote disk hit into memory
        return bitmap
    }

    val bitmap = network.downloadImage(url)
    diskCache.put(url, bitmap)
    memoryCache.put(url, bitmap)
    return bitmap
}
```

The **promotion** step — writing a disk-cache hit back into the memory cache — is easy to forget and costs real, repeated disk I/O if skipped: without it, every access to an image that's only in disk cache pays disk-read latency again and again, even on the tenth time viewing the same image in one session, instead of hitting memory after the first promotion.

A disk cache with no eviction policy or size cap grows forever — every image, every API response ever cached stays on disk indefinitely, slowly filling the user's device storage over weeks or months of use. Users notice this as 'this app takes up way more storage than it should,' and on a device with limited storage, it can crowd out space the user actually wants for photos or other apps, generating real complaints and uninstalls.

The fix is a bounded cache with an explicit eviction policy — a maximum size (in bytes or item count) with LRU (least-recently-used) eviction once the cap is hit, which most platform-provided caching libraries (Android's `DiskLruCache`, various iOS caching libraries) implement out of the box rather than requiring a hand-rolled solution. The cap itself should be a deliberate product decision (a few hundred MB is common for an image-heavy app), not an afterthought left unset.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: prefetching aggressively on a metered connection
slides.markdown:
Prefetching's whole value proposition — spend bandwidth speculatively to eliminate a future delay — inverts into a real user complaint when it runs unconditionally on a metered cellular connection with a limited data plan: the app burns a user's data allowance downloading content they may never actually view, and users on a tight data plan notice this specifically and rate it poorly.

The fix is checking the actual connection type and, ideally, a user-configurable preference before prefetching: prefetch aggressively on Wi-Fi (effectively free, high-bandwidth), throttle or disable it on cellular by default, and respect an explicit 'data saver' setting if the platform or app exposes one. Treating all connections as equally cheap to speculate on is the specific mistake — the fix isn't 'never prefetch,' it's 'prefetch conditioned on the actual cost of being wrong.'

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: cache correctness before cache performance
slides.markdown:
A junior answer optimizes purely for hit rate — bigger cache, longer TTL, more prefetching, all in service of fewer network calls. A senior answer treats **correctness** (never confidently showing data that's actually wrong) as the higher-priority constraint, and tunes performance within it — a cache that's blazingly fast but occasionally shows a stale price or a deleted item as still present is worse for the product than a slightly slower one that's always right.

The concrete discipline this implies: pick each data type's invalidation strategy from its actual staleness tolerance first (as in the strategy-selection slide above), and only then optimize hit rate and prefetch aggressiveness within whatever correctness constraint that choice implies. Optimizing hit rate before deciding what correctness requires is how caches end up serving confidently wrong data in production.
